name: Syrian

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Syrian minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 24 sourced topics and 8 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 15 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

secondary_centers: Safed and Jerusalem (close ties from the 16th century)

languages: Arabic: the community grew from native Arabic-speaking (Musta'arabi) Jews and Sephardi exiles
Judeo-Arabic: the Pesach table exchange and the Judeo-Arabic translation of the Torah (Sharh)

subgroups.name: Aleppo (Halabi)
subgroups.note: Jews of Aleppo (Halab, Hebrew Aram Soba). The community was formed from native Arabic-speaking (Musta'arabi) Jews and Sephardi exiles who came after 1492. Most of the documented customs here come from this subgroup, mainly through the minhag book Derech Eretz as cited by Rabbi Eli Mansour.

subgroups.name: Damascus (Shami)
subgroups.note: Jews of Damascus (al-Sham). Historically they had separate synagogues and schools and married separately from Halabis. Their documented customs here are limited to a separate bakashot order and 16th-century legal customs. Modern Shami ritual differences are mostly undocumented in the sources consulted.

subgroups.name: US diaspora (Brooklyn / Deal, NJ)
subgroups.note: Size estimates vary: 75,000 (Wikipedia, 'Syrian Jews'); about 90,000 for the New York and New Jersey communities in 2007 (Wikipedia, 'Syrian Jewish communities of the United States'); or 'more than 50,000, mostly in Brooklyn and Deal, N.J.' by the community's own count (JTA, 2004). Centered around Ocean Parkway, Brooklyn, with a satellite community in Deal, NJ. Halabi and Shami descendants now intermarry freely. Shared institutions include the 1935 Edict, the 1964 'Shir Ushbaha Hallel VeZimrah' pizmonim book and the rulings of Hakhamim Kassin, Ben Haim and Mansour.

timeline.event: The community identifies Aleppo with Aram Soba and Damascus with Aram Dameseq, both conquered by King David.
timeline.halachic_impact: This is the basis for treating Aleppo as having partial Land-of-Israel status for some laws. Per Wikipedia only, some such laws extend to Aleppo but not Damascus. Needs review.

timeline.event: Sephardi exiles arrive after 1492. Damascus has close ties to Safed and Jerusalem, and in doubtful cases local practice relied on 'minhag Dameshek'.
timeline.halachic_impact: Separate Sephardi groups in Aleppo, the 'Kahal Kadosh Sepharadim', kept Spanish customs such as the extra Chanukah candle. Damascus ketubah and inheritance customs were cited across the region.

timeline.event: The Sabbatean movement wins followers in Syria.
timeline.halachic_impact: According to Rabbi Mansour, the Hakhamim cut back messianic references in the liturgy, which is why the four 'Halevi' stanzas of Lecha Dodi are omitted.

timeline.event: Mass emigration to New York, first to Manhattan, then Brooklyn.
timeline.halachic_impact: Halabi and Shami immigrants first kept separate synagogues, schools and marriages.

timeline.event: Chief Rabbi Jacob Kassin and four rabbis, including Bet Din head Hakham Haim Tawil, issue the Proclamation (Edict) on converts. It was clarified in 1946 and 1972 and reaffirmed in 1984.
timeline.halachic_impact: The community does not accept converts for marriage. In current practice this has been extended into a blanket ban.

timeline.event: 'Shir Ushbaha Hallel VeZimrah' (the Red pizmonim book) is published in Jerusalem for the Aleppo community of Brooklyn.
timeline.halachic_impact: It became the community's standard pizmonim collection and the reference for the weekly maqam.

timeline.event: Year-round settlement in Deal, NJ: in the 1970s it 'lured tens of families to buy homes in the Deal area', and it now has 'hundreds of families in the winter months and thousands in the summer' (Gina Doueck, Conversations 29). According to Doueck, 'The last wave of immigrants arrived in the 1990s', and 'the number of Jews in Syria today is five or fewer persons.' A trend toward Haredi practice follows.
timeline.halachic_impact: Gina Doueck (Conversations 29) contrasts 'the traditional, more practical approach' of Hakhamim Haim Tawil (1860–1942), Matloub Abadi (1887–1970) and Jacob Kassin (1900–1994) with Haredi practices brought in from Lakewood and Israel, such as 'full-time learning in kollel, women using wigs for hair covering instead of the traditional snood'.

primary_codes: Writings and customs of the Arizal (R. Yitzhak Luria), followed where they differ from Maran (e.g., Kapparot)
major_rishonim_base: Rambam (historically influential in Aleppo; some Halab prayer books follow his Chanukah blessing text)
later_poskim: Ben Ish Hai (R. Yosef Haim of Baghdad)
Eretz Haim (R. Haim Sutton of Aleppo)
Derech Eretz (minhag book of the Aleppo community)
Hakham Jacob S. Kassin (Chief Rabbi, Brooklyn)
Rabbi Eli J. Mansour (Edmond J. Safra Synagogue, Brooklyn; Ohel Yaacob, Deal)
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Shulchan Aruch as the base. Kabbalistic practice of the Arizal, as transmitted by the Ben Ish Hai and Kaf HaHaim, is followed where the two conflict. Specific Aleppo customs recorded in Derech Eretz and the Halab siddurim are kept where they exist. Rabbi Mansour states: 'We, of course, treat all the customs and practices of the Arizal with the utmost seriousness and respect, as they reflect the customs of the Kabbalistic tradition, which we follow.'

runtime.practice_baseline: Practice rests on the Shulchan Aruch read through the Arizal, the Ben Ish Hai and the Kaf HaHaim, together with specific Aleppo customs (Derech Eretz, Eretz Haim) as taught in the US by Hakhamim Kassin, Ben Haim and Rabbi Eli Mansour.

halacha_index.summary: Syrian synagogues pray from 'Aram Soba' (Aleppo) siddurim. The Kol Yaakob siddur is cited as a source for Halab custom. The rite is Sephardi and Kabbalistic, following the Arizal where he differs from the Shulchan Aruch.
common_practices: Siddurim 'keminhag Aram Soba' in Brooklyn synagogues
Kol Yaakob weekday siddur cited as a record of Halab custom
Arizal's customs followed over Maran where they conflict

variants.practice: Its liturgy is reported to differ from Aleppo's 'in some details, mostly because of its greater proximity to the Holy Land'.

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, 'Select Halachot on Yom Kippur' (DailyHalacha archive, 2015), section 'The Custom of Kapparot'; Hanna Zemer, 'Nusach Aram Soba – Halab she-be-Flatbush' (1995)
halacha_index.review_notes: The Zemer essay was seen only as a search excerpt. The detailed textual differences between the Aleppo and Damascus siddurim are a gap.

halacha_index.summary_he: בתי הכנסת הסוריים מתפללים מסידורי "ארם צובא" (חלב). הסידור "קול יעקב" מצוטט כמקור למנהג חלב. הנוסח ספרדי וקבלי, והולך אחרי האר"י כשהוא חולק על השולחן ערוך.

halacha_index.summary: Friday night begins with Psalm 29 (Mizmor LeDavid Havu) and goes straight to Lecha Dodi, without Ana BeKho'ah. Next come Mizmor Shir and Hashem Malach with no Kaddish, then Kol Yisrael, Bameh Madlikin and 'Rabbi Hananya ben Akashya' (not 'Amar Rabbi Elazar'). Kaddish Al Yisrael follows, then Mizmor Shir and Hashem Malach again, said seated, then Kaddish seated. The congregation stands for Barechu, when the extra Shabbat soul is received.
common_practices: No Ana BeKho'ah before Lecha Dodi
Mizmor Shir / Hashem Malach recited twice, the second time seated
Stand for Barechu

variants.practice: Described as 'still observed by the Syrian Jewish community today'.

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, DailyHalacha.com, 'The Friday Night Prayer Service According to the Custom of Halab' (id 2341)
halacha_index.review_notes: Single detailed source for Aleppo/US. Damascus order not found.
halacha_index.summary_he: ליל שבת מתחיל במזמור כט ("הבו לה'") ועובר ישר ל"לכה דודי", בלי "אנא בכוח". אחר כך באים "מזמור שיר" ו"ה' מלך" בלי קדיש, ואחריהם "כל ישראל", "במה מדליקין" ו"רבי חנניה בן עקשיא" (לא "אמר רבי אלעזר"). אחר כך קדיש על ישראל, ואחריו שוב "מזמור שיר" ו"ה' מלך" בישיבה, ואז קדיש בישיבה. הקהל עומד ל"ברכו", כשמקבלים את הנשמה היתרה של שבת.

halacha_index.topic: Lecha Dodi: omission of the four 'Halevi' stanzas
halacha_index.summary: Syrian custom omits the stanzas Hitna'ari, Lo Teboshi, VeHayu LiMshisa and Yamin USmol, which spell 'Halevi'. Only the stanzas spelling 'Shlomo' are sung. The reason given is the Sabbatean episode: the Hakhamim cut back explicit messianic references.
common_practices: Lecha Dodi ends with the stanza beginning 'Hit'oreri'
halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, DailyHalacha.com id 2341
halacha_index.review_notes: Stated as 'the custom in Syria', but documented from one source. Whether Damascus followed it is not separately confirmed.
halacha_index.summary_he: המנהג הסורי משמיט את הבתים "התנערי", "לא תבושי", "והיו למשיסה" ו"ימין ושמאל", המרכיבים את השם "הלוי". שרים רק את הבתים המרכיבים "שלמה". הסיבה הניתנת היא פרשת השבתאות: החכמים צמצמו אזכורים משיחיים מפורשים.

halacha_index.topic: Weekly maqam (melodic mode) for Shabbat prayers
halacha_index.summary: A different Arabic maqam is used each Shabbat for Shaharit, chosen by the theme of the parasha, following the Red pizmonim book 'Shir Ushbaha Hallel VeZimrah'. The main maqamat are Rast, Mahour, Ajam, Nahwand, Saba, Sigah, Bayat, Hoseni, Rahawi/Nawah and Hijaz. Pizmonim melodies are fitted to the prayers.
common_practices: Hazzan applies the maqam of the week on Shabbat; not applied on weekdays
High Holiday melodies are older and drawn from Golden-Age piyyutim and Selihot (list on p. 569 of the Red book)

variants.practice: 'Slight variations in the maqam choices by the Beirut...' traditions are noted. The Damascus-specific choices are not recorded here.
variants.source: Sephardic Pizmonim Project, 'Maqam of the Week, Book of Numbers' (2009)

halacha_index.source: Sephardic Pizmonim Project, 'Maqam of the Week: Book of Numbers – Summer 2009' and 'High Holidays' festival page
halacha_index.review_notes: The maqam assignments for each parasha are in the Pizmonim Project tables. The app should pull them from there rather than this summary.

halacha_index.summary_he: בכל שבת משתמשים במקאם ערבי אחר לשחרית, הנבחר לפי נושא הפרשה, לפי ספר הפזמונים האדום "שיר ושבחה הלל וזמרה". המקאמות העיקריים הם ראסט, מאהור, עג'ם, נהאוונד, סבא, סיגה, בייאת, חוסייני, רהאווי/נוואה וחיג'אז. ניגוני הפזמונים מותאמים לתפילות.

halacha_index.summary: On winter Shabbat mornings Aleppian congregations gather before dawn to sing a fixed cycle of bakashot until Shaharit. The text is the same every week and opens with 'El Mistater'. It follows a maqam system that changes from week to week, with poems from the Spanish Golden Age and by Aleppo poets. In the Aleppian tradition the season runs from Sukkot to Shabbat HaGadol.
common_practices: Begins well before dawn on winter Shabbatot
Fixed text each week (unlike the Moroccan weekly cycle)
Passed down orally from paytan to student
Collection: Miqra Qodesh, compiled by Rabbi Mordechai Abadi in Aleppo in 1872 (Hadar Cohen, The New Arab)

variants.practice: Practised from Shabbat Bereshit until Shabbat HaGadol.
variants.source: Hebrew University Jewish Music Research Centre, 'Baqqashah (Pl. Baqqashot)'

variants.practice: Had its own printed order, 'Baqashot of Shabbat', Beirut 1913 (Damascus tradition). It opens with the petiha 'El Yaqshib LaQol Tahanunai', includes 'Qabel Tefilati' and omits 'Ani Ashava' and 'Odeh El Hai', which appear in the Aleppo editions.
variants.source: Sephardic Pizmonim Project, Baqashot section comparison table (pizmonim.com/section.php?maqam=Baqashot)

variants.practice: JTA (May 6, 2014) quotes organizer Thomas saying bakashot 'have also experienced a resurgence in the local Syrian community'. The article adds that among Syrian Jews 'there is a set group of 66 bakashot that are recited completely or in part each week.'
variants.source: JTA, 'Bringing back bakashot' (May 6, 2014), via The Jewish Standard

halacha_index.source: Hibba Center / Zalman Shazar Center, 'The Baqashot Tradition of Aleppo's Jewish Community'; HUJI Jewish Music Research Centre; IEMJ 'Baqqachot'
halacha_index.review_notes: Sources disagree on the season. The HUJI source gives Sukkot to Shabbat HaGadol for Aleppians. Wikipedia ('Baqashot') says 'from the Jewish festival of Sukkot through Purim', and JTA (2014) says 'in the months between Sukkot and Passover'. One AI-written encyclopedia claims Damascus had no bakashot, which the 1913 Damascus-tradition book contradicts.

halacha_index.summary_he: בבקרי שבת של החורף מתכנסות קהילות חלביות לפני עלות השחר לשיר מחזור קבוע של בקשות עד שחרית. הנוסח זהה בכל שבוע ופותח ב"אל מסתתר". הוא הולך לפי מערכת מקאמים המשתנה משבוע לשבוע, עם שירים מתור הזהב של ספרד ושל משוררי חלב. במסורת החלבית העונה נמשכת מסוכות עד שבת הגדול.

halacha_index.summary: Following the Ben Ish Hai, the order is: date (with HaEtz covering all tree fruits), any HaAdama food (covering the rest), then Lubia (black-eyed peas, the community's custom instead of Rubia) with the word 'She'telabebenu' in the Yehi Ratzon. Next come leek (Karti), Swiss chard, gourd, pomegranate and apple, then sheep's head or fish head according to family custom. The Yehi Ratzon is said after taking a bite, to avoid an interruption.
common_practices: Lubia rather than Rubia
Over the apple the word 'Ki'dbash' is omitted: 'Shana Tova U'mutka Me'reshit Shana Ve'ad Aharit Shana'
Some dip the apple in sugar rather than honey (Ben Ish Hai); follow family custom
One who cannot eat a siman looks at or points to it and says the Yehi Ratzon (Kaf HaHaim)
Eaten on the first night; some do both nights

variants.practice: Lubia, and the shortened apple formula without Ki'dbash, are described as 'our community's custom' / 'our custom'.
variants.source: Mansour, Select Halachot on Rosh Hashana (2020), p. 11

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, 'Select Halachot on Rosh Hashana' (iTorah archive, Sept. 14, 2020), 'The Order of the Simanim', p. 11; 'One Who Cannot Eat the Traditional Rosh Hashanah Foods', p. 10
halacha_index.review_notes: Mansour says the order 'is not critical'. Aleppo- or Damascus-specific orders before emigration were not found.

halacha_index.summary_he: לפי הבן איש חי הסדר הוא: תמר (כשברכת "העץ" פוטרת את כל פירות העץ), כל מאכל "האדמה" (הפוטר את השאר), ואחר כך לוביא (שעועית שחורת עין, מנהג הקהילה במקום רוביא) עם המילה "שנתלבבנו" ב"יהי רצון". אחר כך באים כרתי, תרד עלים, דלעת, רימון ותפוח, ואחר כך ראש כבש או ראש דג לפי מנהג המשפחה. ה"יהי רצון" נאמר אחרי נגיסה, כדי למנוע הפסק.

halacha_index.summary: Although the Shulchan Aruch (following the Rashba) calls for abolishing Kapparot, the community follows the Arizal and performs it with a chicken: a rooster for each male, a hen for each female, and for a pregnant woman one hen for herself plus a hen and a rooster for the fetus. The chicken is swung three times while saying 'Zeh Halifati, Zeh Temurati, Zeh Kaparati'. Preferred time is early morning of Ereb Yom Kippur. Money given to charity is an acceptable alternative.
common_practices: Owner covers the blood (Kisui HaDam) with a blessing
Use the formula 'Zeh HaTarnegol Yelech LeMita Ve'ikanes Ani...' (Kaf HaHaim)
Declare it 'beli neder'

variants.practice: Codified by the Aleppo authority Eretz Haim (R. Haim Sutton).
variants.source: Mansour, Select Halachot on Yom Kippur (2015), p. 3

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, 'Select Halachot on Yom Kippur' (DailyHalacha archive, Sept. 19, 2015), 'The Custom of Kapparot', pp. 3–4
halacha_index.review_notes: This contradicts Shulchan Aruch OC 605 on purpose, following the Arizal.

references.title: Daily Halacha Podcast - Daily Halacha By Rabbi Eli J. Mansour

halacha_index.summary_he: אף שהשולחן ערוך (בעקבות הרשב"א) קורא לבטל את הכפרות, הקהילה הולכת אחרי האר"י ומקיימת אותן בתרנגול: תרנגול לכל זכר, תרנגולת לכל נקבה, ולאישה הרה תרנגולת אחת בעבורה ועוד תרנגולת ותרנגול בעבור העובר. מניפים את העוף שלוש פעמים ואומרים "זה חליפתי, זה תמורתי, זה כפרתי". הזמן המועדף הוא בוקר מוקדם של ערב יום כיפור. כסף שניתן לצדקה הוא חלופה מקובלת.

halacha_index.summary: In Halab the accepted custom was either not to light Yom Kippur candles or to light them without a blessing. When Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat, the blessing 'LeHadlik Ner Shel Shabbat VeYom HaKippurim' is said.
common_practices: No blessing on weekday Yom Kippur candles (Halab custom)
Women who are not in synagogue for Kal Nidre still say Shehehiyanu

variants.practice: No blessing is said, even when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat.

variants.subgroup: The consensus view, according to Rabbi Mansour
variants.practice: The blessing is said when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat.

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, 'Select Halachot on Yom Kippur' (2015), 'Candle Lighting', p. 22, citing Derech Eretz and the Kol Yaakob weekday siddur
halacha_index.review_notes: The wording was read from search excerpts of this PDF and the DailyHalacha podcast page; the fetched copy was cut off before p. 22. Needs to be checked against the full text.
halacha_index.summary_he: בחלב המנהג המקובל היה שלא להדליק נרות ליום כיפור או להדליק אותם בלי ברכה. כשיום כיפור חל בשבת אומרים את הברכה "להדליק נר של שבת ושל יום הכיפורים".

halacha_index.summary: In Rabbi Mansour's words, 'There is a custom observed by some Jews with roots in Aleppo to light an extra candle each night of Hanukah': three on the first night (one for the mitzvah and two 'shamash'), four on the second, and so on. Derech Eretz says the custom belonged specifically to the 'Kahal Kadosh Sepharadim', the Aleppo group that kept Spanish customs.
common_practices: The extra candle is placed away from or higher than the mitzvah candles
Those whose forebears did not keep it light the standard number

variants.practice: Light the extra candle. Derech Eretz gives two reasons in the name of R. Yitzhak Tawil: (1) these wealthy families normally kept two lamps lit, so two Chanukah lights would not be noticed; (2) concern about 'zugot' (pairs).
Mansour (#745) says the extra candle should not be placed in the menorah, and should be lit only after the whole lighting, including Hanerot Halalu, is finished.
No documentation that Damascus families keep this custom. Sources describe it only for Aleppo.

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, DailyHalacha.com, 'The Custom Among Some Syrian Jews to Light an Extra Candle on Hanukah' (id 2595), citing Derech Eretz
halacha_index.review_notes: The custom is well attested; the reason is disputed. Popular sources say it is gratitude for a refuge after 1492 (Forward; Chabad). #745 attributes it to 'a miracle that happened to Syrian Jews one year'. Derech Eretz gives practical reasons. Do not apply it to every Syrian family.

halacha_index.summary_he: בדברי הרב מנסור, "יש מנהג שמקיימים יהודים מסוימים ששורשיהם בחלב להדליק נר נוסף בכל לילה של חנוכה": שלושה בלילה הראשון (אחד למצווה ושניים "שמש"), ארבעה בשני, וכן הלאה. "דרך ארץ" אומר שהמנהג שייך דווקא ל"קהל קדוש ספרדים", קבוצת חלב ששמרה מנהגי ספרד.

halacha_index.summary: The Syrian community says 'LeHadlik Ner Hanukah' (Shulchan Aruch and Arizal), not 'LeHadlik Ner Shel Hanukah', even though the Rambam has 'Shel' and some Halab prayer books follow him. Derech Eretz records no fixed custom for when Hanerot Halalu begins.
common_practices: 'LeHadlik Ner Hanukah'

variants.practice: Some Halab prayer books print 'Ner Shel Hanukah' (Rambam).
variants.source: Mansour, 'Hanukah – The Berachot Over the Candle Lighting' (iTorah)

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, 'Hanukah – The Berachot Over the Candle Lighting', iTorah.com lecture 20275
halacha_index.review_notes: Read from a search excerpt of the lecture text, not the full page.
halacha_index.summary_he: הקהילה הסורית אומרת "להדליק נר חנוכה" (שולחן ערוך והאר"י), ולא "להדליק נר של חנוכה", אף שלרמב"ם יש "של" וסידורי חלב אחדים הולכים אחריו. "דרך ארץ" אינו מתעד מנהג קבוע לגבי המועד שבו מתחילים "הנרות הללו".

halacha_index.summary: In Aleppo the congregation sings five verses of the Megillah aloud, in the Aleppo Megillah melody: 'Ish Yehudi', 'BaLaila HaHu', 'UMordechai Yatza', 'LaYehudim Hayta Ora' and 'Ki Mordechai HaYehudi'. Most communities read only the first four aloud.
common_practices: Congregation sings the verses in the Megillah melody

variants.practice: The whole community adopted the Musta'arabi customs for the Torah reading and Al HaNissim on both days of Purim. The details are not recorded here.
variants.source: Aleppo Jewry Heritage Center, 'Customs of Halab special to Purim'

halacha_index.source: Aleppo Jewry Heritage Center (Merkaz Moreshet Aram Tzova), 'מנהגי חלב המיוחדים לימי הפורים'
halacha_index.review_notes: The page blocked fetching; content is from the search excerpt only. A related NLI booklet: 'Purim... minhagei Purim shel yehudei Aram Tzova', ed. Moshe Cohen.

references.title: מנהגי חלב המיוחדים לימי הפורים

halacha_index.summary_he: בחלב שר הקהל חמישה פסוקים מהמגילה בקול, בניגון מגילת חלב: "איש יהודי", "בלילה ההוא", "ומרדכי יצא", "ליהודים היתה אורה" ו"כי מרדכי היהודי". רוב הקהילות קוראות בקול רק את הארבעה הראשונים.

halacha_index.summary: Syrian Jews eat rice and kitniyot on Pesach. Rice traditionally accompanies the lamb shanks served at the seder.
common_practices: Rice eaten on Pesach (checked for grain)
Lamb shanks served as an entree, eaten only at Pesach
halacha_index.source: Halachipedia, 'Kitniyot' ('Syrians eat rice on Pesach'); JTA, 'A Syrian Passover seder' (2004)
halacha_index.review_notes: Both read only as search excerpts; neither is a primary Syrian halachic text. The rule for checking rice comes from general Sephardic sources (Peninei Halakha; Star-K), not Syrian ones.

references.title: Kitniyot - Halachipedia

halacha_index.summary_he: יהודי סוריה אוכלים אורז וקטניות בפסח. האורז מלווה במסורת את שוקי הכבש המוגשים בסדר.

halacha_index.summary: The afikoman is wrapped in a napkin or sack and placed with the right hand over the left shoulder while saying 'Misharotam' (Exodus 12:34). The table asks in Judeo-Arabic 'Minwen jaiyeh?' (Where are you coming from?) – 'Mimmisrayim'; 'Lawen rayech?' (Where are you going?) – 'Liyerushalayim'; 'Ishu zawatek?' (What are you carrying?) – 'Matzah'. The sack is passed around the table.
common_practices: Each participant takes a turn
Exchange in Judeo-Arabic

variants.practice: Family version from Aleppo transcribed by Asher Shasho Levy; it is done after the leader breaks the middle matzah.
variants.source: Jewish Language Project, 'Other Parts of Haggadah'

halacha_index.source: Sarina Roffe, Community Magazine, reprinted as 'Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews' (Point of No Return, Jan. 2018)
halacha_index.review_notes: Roffe contrasts this with the Moroccan practice of waving the seder plate overhead ('Bibhilu'). Do not attribute Bibhilu to Syrians.

references.title: Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews • Point of No Return

halacha_index.summary_he: האפיקומן עטוף במפית או בשק ומונח ביד ימין מעל הכתף השמאלית תוך אמירת "משארותם" (שמות יב:לד). השולחן שואל ביהודית-ערבית "מנוין ג'איה?" (מאין אתה בא?) – "ממצרים"; "לוין ראיח?" (לאן אתה הולך?) – "לירושלים"; "איש זוואתק?" (מה אתה נושא?) – "מצה". השק עובר סביב השולחן.

halacha_index.summary: Firstborn males are exempted by attending a seudat mitzvah on Ereb Pesah. In the Syrian community firstborn women do not fast.
common_practices: Siyum or seudat mitzvah after Shaharit
halacha_index.source: Sarina Roffe, 'Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews' (Community Magazine)
halacha_index.review_notes: One journalistic source.
halacha_index.summary_he: בכורים זכרים נפטרים בהשתתפות בסעודת מצווה בערב פסח. בקהילה הסורית בכורות נשים אינן צמות.

halacha_index.summary: The Sephardic custom taught in the community is that men do not cut their hair until the morning of the 34th day of the Omer (not the night before). Weddings preferably wait until the night after the 34th. Three-year-old boys may have their first haircut on Lag BaOmer itself. Women are not restricted.
common_practices: Haircuts from the morning of the 34th
Father, mohel and sandak may cut their hair for a brit; the father may also for a pidyon haben

variants.practice: Mansour also records that 'some Sephardim' do not cut their hair until Erev Shavuot (the Arizal's practice).

variants.subgroup: Sephardic custom taught in the community
variants.practice: Men do not cut their hair until the morning of the 34th day of the Omer.
variants.source: DailyHalacha (Mansour), 'When are Haircuts Allowed During the Omer?'

halacha_index.source: Rabbi Eli J. Mansour, DailyHalacha.com, 'When are Haircuts Allowed During the Omer?' (id 2694); 'Lag Ba'omer: Haircuts...' (readID 269)
halacha_index.review_notes: Presented as general Sephardic custom (Shulchan Aruch OC 493:2), not specifically Halabi or Shami. Read from search excerpts.

references.title: When are Haircuts Allowed During the Omer?
This year Lag B’omer will be on Sunday. When am I permitted to get a haircut?

halacha_index.summary_he: המנהג הספרדי הנלמד בקהילה הוא שגברים אינם גוזרים שיער עד בוקר היום ה-34 בעומר (לא בלילה שלפניו). חתונות ממתינות רצוי עד הלילה שאחרי ה-34. ילדים בני שלוש רשאים לקבל תספורת ראשונה בל"ג בעומר עצמו. נשים אינן מוגבלות.

halacha_index.topic: Aliyah divisions and the Judeo-Arabic Sharh
halacha_index.summary: Aleppo has its own set of stopping points for aliyot, published by Hakham Yosef Mosseri (Brooklyn) in the tikkun korim 'Birkat Abraham' (Sephardic Heritage Foundation). Aleppo also had its own Judeo-Arabic translation of the Torah (Sharh), edited by Prof. Yitzhak Avishur.
common_practices: Stopping points for each aliyah follow minhag Aram Soba
The Pizmonim Project publishes the 'proper Syrian Torah Aliyot Stops'
halacha_index.source: Aleppo Jewry Heritage Center, 'Aliyot in the Torah reading according to minhag Aram Soba' (from 'Birkat Abraham', H. Yosef Mosseri); Y. Avishur, 'The Aleppo Sharh of the Torah'
halacha_index.review_notes: Read from search excerpts only. Pronunciation and trope are a gap.

references.title: עליות בקריאת ספר תורה לפי מנהג ארם צובא

halacha_index.summary_he: לחלב יש מערכת משלה של נקודות עצירה לעליות, שפרסם החכם יוסף מוסרי (ברוקלין) בתיקון קוראים "ברכת אברהם" (קרן המורשת הספרדית). לחלב היה גם תרגום משלה של התורה ליהודית-ערבית (שרח), בעריכת פרופ' יצחק אבישור.

halacha_index.topic: Seniyet Eliyahu HaNabi and other brit customs
halacha_index.summary: At every brit a two-level tray with candles, 'Seniyet Eliyahu HaNabi', is passed around. Guests light candles and give charity, and some take a coin for good mazal. The grandmother carrying the baby wears a gold-threaded family shawl passed down through generations of women. Knafe is the customary food.
common_practices: Candle tray of Eliyahu HaNabi
Heirloom family shawl worn by the grandmother
Knafe served
halacha_index.source: Sarina Roffe, 'Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews' (Community Magazine)
halacha_index.review_notes: One source. Roffe says she has never seen the shawl custom written about and calls it a family custom ('among many Jewish families'), so it is not universal.
halacha_index.summary_he: בכל ברית מעבירים מגש דו-קומתי עם נרות, "סניית אליהו הנביא". אורחים מדליקים נרות ונותנים צדקה, ויש הלוקחים מטבע למזל טוב. הסבתא הנושאת את התינוק עוטה צעיף משפחתי רקום חוטי זהב שעובר בדורות של נשים. הכנאפה היא המאכל המקובל.

halacha_index.summary: The grandmother wears the same heirloom family shawl when a firstborn son is brought for redemption by the Kohen.
halacha_index.source: Sarina Roffe, 'Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews' (Community Magazine)
halacha_index.review_notes: Family custom, one source.
halacha_index.summary_he: הסבתא עוטה את אותו צעיף המשפחה היקר כשבן בכור מובא לפדיון אצל הכהן.

halacha_index.summary: In Syria the groom's side sent money to the bride for her pre-wedding mikveh visit. This grew into the swanee: gifts (nightgown, perfume, evening bag, jewelry) on decorated trays with white flowers and sugared almonds, displayed at the bride's home at a tea or evening party. Today the bride's mother also sends gifts to the groom.
common_practices: Gift trays displayed at the bride's home
Often combined with an American bridal shower
Engagement foods: shob el boz (cornstarch pudding) and maziye (almond drink)

variants.practice: Gifts are now also given to the groom (e.g., a tallit bag).

halacha_index.source: Sarina Roffe, 'Rich traditions unique to Syrian Jews' (Community Magazine)
halacha_index.review_notes: The name is probably from Arabic 'seniyeh' (tray), per community forum comments, which are not authoritative.
halacha_index.summary_he: בסוריה שלח צד החתן כסף לכלה לביקורה במקווה לפני החתונה. מכאן התפתח הסוואני: מתנות (כתונת לילה, בושם, תיק ערב, תכשיטים) על מגשים מקושטים בפרחים לבנים ושקדים מסוכרים, המוצגים בבית הכלה בתה או במסיבת ערב. כיום שולחת גם אם הכלה מתנות לחתן.

halacha_index.summary: In February 1935 (Adar 5695) Chief Rabbi Jacob Kassin and four rabbis, including Bet Din head Hakham Haim Tawil, proclaimed that 'no male or female member of our community has the right to intermarry with non-Jews; this law covers conversions, which we consider to be fictitious and valueless', and that no community rabbinic court may convert non-Jews who seek to marry in. The 1946 clarification: 'Our community will never accept any converts, male or female, for marriage. The rabbi will not perform any religious ceremonies for such couples.' It was reaffirmed in 1972 and 1984.
common_practices: Current practice is a full ban on marriage with converts, including descendants of converts married by Rabbi Kassin

variants.practice: Rabbi Zevulun Lieberman (1988): 'Our ban... does not apply to descendants of people who underwent a legitimate conversion prior to 1935.' A disciple of Rabbi Kassin says he married sincere converts. Current practice is stricter than either.
A blanket exclusion of converts, including descendants of converts married by Rabbi Kassin.

halacha_index.source: Gina Doueck (pen name), 'The Syrian Jewish Community, Then and Now', Conversations issue 29 (Institute for Jewish Ideas and Ideals)
halacha_index.review_notes: The edict itself is well attested. Its scope (marriage-motivated conversions only, or all converts and descendants) is disputed between its original wording and current practice. It covers the US community, not historical Aleppo or Damascus.

references.title: Syrian Jewish Community in North America - UPG North America

halacha_index.summary_he: בפברואר 1935 (אדר תרצ"ה) הכריזו הרב הראשי יעקב קסין וארבעה רבנים, ובהם ראש בית הדין החכם חיים טוויל, ש"אין לשום חבר או חברה בקהילתנו זכות להינשא לגויים; חוק זה מכסה גיורים, שאנו רואים בהם פיקטיביים וחסרי ערך", וש"אסור לשום בית דין קהילתי לגייר גויים המבקשים להינשא לקהילה". ההבהרה של 1946: "קהילתנו לא תקבל לעולם גרים או גיורות לנישואין. הרב לא יקיים שום טקס דתי לזוגות כאלה". היא אושרה מחדש ב-1972 וב-1984.

halacha_index.summary: In Syria and among first-generation US immigrants, Shami and Halabi Jews kept separate schools, synagogues and marriages. Second-generation immigrants mixed and intermarried. Today there are few if any objections, and marriages with Ashkenazim are increasing.

variants.practice: Historically married within the group.
Historically married within the group.

halacha_index.source: Gina Doueck, 'The Syrian Jewish Community, Then and Now', Conversations 29
halacha_index.review_notes: Social custom, not halacha.

references.title: Syrian Jews
Lyn Julius The Jews of Syria

halacha_index.summary_he: בסוריה ובקרב מהגרים בני הדור הראשון בארצות הברית שמרו יהודי שאם וחלב על בתי ספר, בתי כנסת ונישואין נפרדים. בני הדור השני התערבבו והתחתנו זה עם זה. כיום יש מעט התנגדויות, אם בכלל, והנישואין עם אשכנזים הולכים וגדלים.

halacha_index.summary: In the 16th century the Damascus ketubah had both an up-front and a deferred payment ('mukdam u-me'uhar'). Under the old Land-of-Israel/Damascus enactment a wife's heirs shared equally; the Safed sages replaced this so her heirs took one third. Other towns relied on 'minhag Dameshek' in doubtful cases, and Jerusalem's custom is described as being like Damascus's.

variants.practice: Historical legal custom.

halacha_index.source: Eliezer and Yosef Yoel Rivlin, 'Le-korot ha-Yehudim be-Dameshek ba-me'ah ha-revi'it la-elef ha-shishi', Reshumot (Dvir, 1926), Project Ben-Yehuda
halacha_index.review_notes: Historical (16th c.); not evidence of current Shami practice. Key passages came to the research subagent via search excerpts.
halacha_index.summary_he: במאה ה-16 הייתה בכתובת דמשק תשלום מראש ותשלום נדחה ("מוקדם ומאוחר"). לפי התקנה הישנה של ארץ ישראל/דמשק חלקו יורשי האישה שווה בשווה; חכמי צפת החליפו אותה בכך שיורשיה לקחו שליש. ערים אחרות נשענו על "מנהג דמשק" במקרים מסופקים, ומנהג ירושלים מתואר כדומה למנהג דמשק.

halacha_index.summary: In the Syrian community a memorial meal and study session (Arayat or Mishmara) with a eulogy is held at the end of shiva, at 30 days, at the end of the (11-month) year and on each anniversary, usually in the synagogue. Visitors to the shiva house are commonly offered breakfast after prayers and refreshments through the day. Visitors say a blessing for the elevation of the soul when they eat.
common_practices: Arayat at the end of shiva, at 30 days, at the year's end and annually
Food offered to shiva visitors
halacha_index.source: Mona Daniella blog, category 'Mishmara "Arayat"'
halacha_index.review_notes: A single non-rabbinic blog, read via search excerpt. Must be checked against a rabbinic source before publishing.
halacha_index.summary_he: בקהילה הסורית נערכת סעודת זיכרון ומושב לימוד (ערייאת או משמרה) עם הספד בסוף השבעה, בשלושים, בסוף השנה (של אחד עשר החודשים) ובכל יום שנה, בדרך כלל בבית הכנסת. למבקרים בבית השבעה מציעים בדרך כלל ארוחת בוקר אחרי התפילה וכיבוד במשך היום. המבקרים אומרים ברכה לעילוי הנשמה כשהם אוכלים.

halacha_index.summary: Pizmonim (para-liturgical hymns) arranged by maqam form the community's song repertoire for life-cycle and synagogue use. The US standard is 'Shir Ushbaha Hallel VeZimrah' (the Red book), published in Jerusalem in 1964 for Brooklyn's Aleppo community, based on Hakham Raphael Haim Cohen's 'Shir Ushbaha' (Jerusalem 1905/1921).
common_practices: Pizmonim melodies used for prayer texts on Shabbat and festivals
The Sephardic Pizmonim Project preserves recordings (Hazzan Gabriel A. Shrem collection)
halacha_index.source: Sephardic Pizmonim Project, 'Introduction' index (pizmonim.com) and 'Overview: Welcome'
halacha_index.review_notes: Wikipedia gives 1959 as the year compilation started; pizmonim.org gives 1964 as the publication year. These describe different events.

references.title: Syrian Jews
Pizmonim
Pizmonim.org - Introduction

halacha_index.summary_he: פזמונים (מזמורים פרה-ליטורגיים) המסודרים לפי מקאם הם רפרטואר השירה של הקהילה לשימוש במחזור החיים ובבית הכנסת. התקן בארצות הברית הוא "שיר ושבחה הלל וזמרה" (הספר האדום), שיצא בירושלים ב-1964 לקהילת חלב בברוקלין, על פי "שיר ושבחה" של החכם רפאל חיים כהן (ירושלים 1905/1921).

unique_minhagim.name: Extra Chanukah candle (second shamash)
unique_minhagim.description: One extra candle each night, kept by Aleppo families descended from the 'Kahal Kadosh Sepharadim'. It is placed apart from the mitzvah candles.

unique_minhagim.name: Winter Shabbat bakashot
unique_minhagim.description: Pre-dawn singing of a fixed bakashot cycle opening with 'El Mistater', organized by maqam. Damascus had a separate order (Beirut 1913).
unique_minhagim.when: Winter Shabbatot, Sukkot to Shabbat HaGadol (Aleppo)

unique_minhagim.name: Maqam of the week

unique_minhagim.description: Afikoman carried on the shoulder, with a Judeo-Arabic exchange: 'Minwen jaiyeh? Mimmisrayim. Lawen rayech? Liyerushalayim.'

unique_minhagim.name: Seniyet Eliyahu HaNabi
unique_minhagim.description: Two-level candle tray passed at a brit; guests light candles and give tzedakah.
unique_minhagim.description_he: מגש נרות דו-קומתי המועבר בברית; אורחים מדליקים נרות ונותנים צדקה.

unique_minhagim.name: Swanee
unique_minhagim.description: Display of gift trays for the bride, and now also for the groom.

unique_minhagim.description_he: הצגת מגשי מתנות לכלה, וכיום גם לחתן.

unique_minhagim.name: Tikkun Hasot in the Aleppo synagogue
unique_minhagim.description: Accounts say the Halab synagogue filled at midnight with men saying Tikkun Hasot, who then stayed to learn Torah.

unique_minhagim.name_he: תיקון חצות בבית הכנסת של חלב
unique_minhagim.description_he: לפי עדויות התמלא בית הכנסת בחלב בחצות בגברים שאמרו תיקון חצות, ואחר כך נשארו ללמוד תורה.

unique_minhagim.name: Damascus 'Red Synagogue' lament
unique_minhagim.description: A lament unique to Damascus Jewry, 'Qissat al-Jami' al-Ahmar' (story of the Red Synagogue).
unique_minhagim.description_he: קינה ייחודית ליהדות דמשק, "קיסת אל-ג'אמע אל-אחמר" (סיפור בית הכנסת האדום).
